alternative: Let MRI's GC own objects: use ObjectSpace::WeakMap and WeakRef for non-owning references and caches, ObjectSpace.define_finalizer only for best-effort cleanup, ensure/explicit close protocols for external resources, and plain references for ownership - a hand-written count cannot release anything.
idiom_name: none - MRI's tracing GC owns lifetime; WeakMap/WeakRef for non-owning references
implementation_notes: CRuby is a tracing collector, not a counting one: objects carry no reference count and Ruby has no deterministic destructor, so release-on-every-path comes from ensure blocks and explicit close protocols. What replaces the classic structure: ordinary references for ownership, ObjectSpace::WeakMap - documented as holding weak references to its keys and values so they can be garbage-collected once nothing else references them - for canonicalisation maps and caches, WeakRef for a non-owning handle that may vanish at any time, and ObjectSpace.define_finalizer only where best-effort cleanup after collection is acceptable. A counter kept in an attribute can model protocol state, but the collector cannot see it and it cannot break cycles.
code_sketch:
CANON = ObjectSpace::WeakMap.new
def intern(obj) = CANON[obj] = obj    # entry vanishes with obj

require "weakref"
ref = WeakRef.new(config)             # non-owning handle
ref.weakref_alive?                    # false once collected
pitfalls: Weak references can die between any two statements: every dereference (weakref_alive?, __getobj__) can fail or return stale data, so callers need a fallback path.
Finalizers run at GC time, may run during shutdown in unpredictable order, and a finalizer closure that captures the object keeps it alive so the finalizer never fires.
A count written in Ruby is pure accounting: it cannot trigger release, cannot break cycles, and every forgotten decrement is a silent bug no test catches reliably.
